explanation.summary: This child had an uncomplicated typical E coli UTI that responded promptly to first-line antibiotics. The RCH cascade for imaging after paediatric UTI is more restrictive than NICE and does not require routine imaging in this setting. Safety-netting for early urine testing during any future febrile illness is the correct plan.
key_points: RCH indications for post-UTI ultrasound: age under 6 months without antenatal imaging, atypical UTI, non-E coli organism, poor response at 48 hours, or recurrent UTI
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and are not in the RCH cascade
Antibiotic prophylaxis has a narrow AU indication and is not first-line for a single typical UTI
explanation.pearls: The single strongest driver of over-investigation of paediatric UTI is applying NICE algorithms in Australia. Anchor to RCH and its atypical-UTI trigger list.

options.rationale: RCH does not recommend routine renal tract ultrasound after a single typical E coli UTI in a child aged over 6 months who responded within 48 hours of antibiotics, has normal antenatal imaging, and no atypical features. Safety-netting for early reassessment of any future febrile illness is the appropriate outpatient plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Routine post-UTI ultrasound is a NICE construct, not the RCH pathway. RCH reserves ultrasound for atypical UTI, recurrence, non-E coli organism, sepsis, or infants under 6 months without antenatal imaging - none apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
DMSA is a NICE-recommended follow-up but does not appear in the RCH cascade. The RCH pathway does not use DMSA for a single typical UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MCUG is invasive, involves urinary catheterisation and ionising radiation, and is not part of the RCH post-UTI cascade for a single typical UTI. It is reserved for selected children with recurrent UTI or abnormal ultrasound findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a single typical E coli UTI in a low-risk child. Trials such as PRIVENT show modest benefit only in selected higher-risk populations, and prophylaxis is not first-line here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses a banded weight rule for paediatric adrenaline autoinjectors: 150 microgram for 7.5 to 20 kg and 300 microgram for 20 kg and above. Two devices should be prescribed together so a repeat dose is available at 5 minutes if needed. This 22 kg boy requires two 300 microgram devices.
key_points: ASCIA banded doses: EpiPen Jr 150 mcg for 7.5 to 20 kg, EpiPen 300 mcg for 20 kg and above
Prescribe two devices simultaneously; the repeat dose is given after 5 minutes if response is inadequate
Oral antihistamines and daily inhaled corticosteroids have no role in preventing anaphylaxis
explanation.pearls: Do not perform mg/kg arithmetic at the bedside for autoinjectors - use the ASCIA weight bands. The threshold of 20 kg is the one to remember.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.rationale: The 150 microgram device is reserved for children weighing 7.5 to 20 kg. At 22 kg this child has crossed into the 300 microgram band. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.rationale: ASCIA prescribes the 300 microgram device for children weighing 20 kg or more using a banded weight rule. Two devices are the standard AU prescription to allow a repeat dose if symptoms do not respond after 5 minutes. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.rationale: ASCIA advises prescribing two devices simultaneously so a second dose is immediately available at the same location if response is inadequate at 5 minutes. Waiting for a second prescription is unsafe. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.rationale: Regular antihistamine has no preventive role in food anaphylaxis and does not reduce risk. It also risks masking early urticarial signs of a reaction. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.rationale: There is no indication for inhaled corticosteroid without a diagnosis of asthma, and 150 microgram is the wrong band for a 22 kg child. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

explanation.summary:
Bloody diarrhoea after a plausible exposure to undercooked beef raises Shiga toxin producing Escherichia coli, and antibiotics in that setting increase the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome by promoting toxin release. Australian practice is therefore supportive: maintain hydration, send stool for culture and molecular testing, avoid antimotility agents, and take a baseline full blood count, blood film and electrolytes so that falling haemoglobin and platelets or rising creatinine are detected. Antibiotics are reserved for organisms and clinical situations where they are known to help.

In context: most acute diarrhoea in Australian children is viral and needs no microbiology at all. Stool testing earns its place when the stool is bloody, the illness is prolonged, the child is immunocompromised, there has been relevant travel, or an outbreak is suspected. Clinicians should also notify enteric pathogens where the state public health requirements apply.
key_points: Avoid antibiotics where Shiga toxin producing infection is plausible
Send stool for culture and molecular testing in bloody diarrhoea
Monitor full blood count, film and electrolytes for haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Antimotility agents are not used in children
explanation.pearls: The reflex to cover bloody diarrhoea with an antibiotic is the exact move that raises the risk of renal failure when the organism is a Shiga toxin producer.

options.rationale: Where Shiga toxin producing Escherichia coli is plausible, Therapeutic Guidelines advises supportive care without antibiotics, with a full blood count, film and electrolytes to watch for haemolytic uraemic syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Azithromycin is the Australian choice for confirmed shigellosis, severe campylobacteriosis, or travellers with dysentery, and is reserved until the organism is known in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This agent is used for susceptible Shigella or for enteric infection in an immunocompromised child; in Shiga toxin producing infection it increases toxin release. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Antimotility agents are not used in children with acute diarrhoea at all, and in invasive infection they prolong exposure to the pathogen and risk ileus. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Parenteral cover is for a child with suspected invasive bacterial disease, sepsis, or who is immunocompromised or under 3 months, none of which applies to a well perfused, alert toddler. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: This child has septic shock with purpuric rash suggestive of meningococcaemia. The RCH pathway requires immediate access, cultures, and first-hour antibiotics, followed by 20 mL/kg saline boluses titrated up to 60 mL/kg. Inotropes come only after fluid-refractoriness. LP is deferred while shock persists.
key_points: Order: access, cultures, first antibiotic, 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
Antibiotics within 1 hour is the AU standard - do not delay for cultures if access is difficult
Adrenaline / noradrenaline reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg crystalloid
explanation.pearls: Meningococcal purpura with shock is a national safety pathway. Cef 100 mg/kg IV up to 2 g is the AU empiric dose.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: A fluid bolus cannot be delivered without access, and cultures should be taken before or with the first antibiotic dose whenever access is available - not after. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: Inotropes are reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg of crystalloid. Starting adrenaline before the first fluid bolus is not the AU sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock and impaired consciousness. It is deferred until the child is haemodynamically stable and neurologically improved. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway sequences access first, then cultures, then first-hour antibiotics, then 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes. Antibiotics must not wait for cultures if cultures cannot be drawn promptly, but with prompt access both can be taken in sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: Dexamethasone is considered adjunctively in pneumococcal meningitis and is given with or before the first antibiotic dose, but it should not replace timely antibiotic delivery in septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

explanation.summary: At 96 hours of age a term neonate with an unconjugated bilirubin of 320 micromol/L and no haemolysis has crossed the phototherapy line on the AU-adapted NICE chart. Treatment is single phototherapy with continued breastfeeding and a 6 hour repeat level. Exchange transfusion is a separate, much higher line reserved for severe or resistant hyperbilirubinaemia.
key_points: Phototherapy threshold at 96 hours in a term infant without haemolysis approximates 310 to 320 micromol/L
Exchange transfusion line is much higher (about 450 micromol/L) and unmet here
Continue breastfeeding with support; do not interrupt for phototherapy alone
explanation.pearls: Read the phototherapy chart by age in hours, not days. The line rises sharply over the first 96 hours and plateaus after that.

sources.label: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.rationale: The exchange transfusion line at 96 hours in a term infant without haemolysis is above 450 micromol/L. Her level is well below this. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding is not recommended in AU practice and can compromise establishment. Phototherapy alongside supported breastfeeding is preferred. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.rationale: The bilirubin level at 96 hours has crossed the phototherapy threshold and cannot be observed with community review only. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.rationale: With DAT negative, blood groups matched, and normal reticulocyte count and haemoglobin, urgent haemolysis screen is not the priority. Phototherapy should not wait for further tests. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.rationale: At 96 hours of age a term infant with no haemolysis crosses the AU-adapted NICE phototherapy line at approximately 310 to 320 micromol/L, warranting single phototherapy and a repeat level to check response. Breastfeeding continues alongside. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

explanation.summary: Prolonged fever with fewer than 4 principal Kawasaki criteria but supportive laboratory features fulfils the incomplete Kawasaki disease pathway. IVIG plus aspirin should be started promptly. Delay beyond day 10 markedly increases the risk of coronary artery aneurysm.
key_points: Incomplete KD: 5 or more days of fever, 2 to 3 principal criteria, plus supportive labs (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, thrombocytosis, sterile pyuria, raised ALT, low albumin)
IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
Do not delay treatment for echocardiogram - the two can proceed in parallel
explanation.pearls: The single strongest predictor of long-term coronary sequelae is IVIG delay past day 10. Recognise the incomplete pattern early.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Fever for 5 or more days with 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory features (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, thrombocytosis, sterile pyuria, elevated ALT, low albumin) meets the AHA incomplete Kawasaki disease pathway. Treatment with IVIG plus aspirin should not wait for the echocardiogram. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Delaying IVIG beyond day 10 doubles the risk of coronary aneurysm. Fever on day 6 with matching criteria warrants treatment now. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Group A streptococcal throat swab is negative and there are no oral or pharyngeal features to support scarlet fever. Antibiotic therapy will not address the underlying vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
Steroids are used as adjuncts to IVIG in high-risk or IVIG-refractory disease, not as first-line monotherapy in AU practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
There are no meningitic features and the presentation over 6 days with mucocutaneous features points to Kawasaki disease, not meningitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: The pre and post ductal saturation differential, four-limb blood pressure gradient, hepatomegaly, and lactic acidosis in a 12-day-old point to a critical left-sided ductal-dependent lesion whose duct is closing. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the duct and restores lower body perfusion; it should be started before any other pharmacological intervention while awaiting retrieval. Passing the pulse oximetry screen does not exclude the diagnosis because the post-ductal saturation is initially maintained by the patent duct.
key_points: Prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 10 ng/kg/min reopens the arterial duct in ductal-dependent lesions
Four-limb blood pressures showing an upper to lower gradient over 20 mmHg suggest coarctation or interrupted arch
The pulse oximetry newborn screen picks up right-sided but not all left-sided lesions - late collapse is possible
explanation.pearls: Any collapsed neonate presenting in the second week should have prostaglandin E1 started empirically while echocardiography is arranged. Apnoea is the main dose-related side effect - be prepared to intubate.

sources.label: Australian Newborn Pulse Oximetry Screening Statement

options.rationale: Sinus tachycardia at 176 with a differential four-limb blood pressure and a chest x-ray consistent with heart failure is not SVT. Adenosine will not correct ductal closure. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

A late-presenting ductal-dependent left-sided lesion such as coarctation or interrupted aortic arch reopens with prostaglandin E1. The infusion is started before intubation or catheter placement in a shocked newborn to restore lower body perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

Inotropes increase myocardial oxygen demand in an unrelieved obstruction. Prostaglandin reopening of the duct treats the underlying cause and is the correct first pharmacological step. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)
Diuresis will worsen an already-hypotensive systemic circulation and does nothing for the closed duct. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

Empirical antibiotics are reasonable adjuncts but do not address the underlying ductal-dependent lesion. Prostaglandin is the single most important pharmacological intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in Australian tertiary practice follows the RCH CPG oxygen escalation ladder. Low-flow nasal cannula oxygen is first-line for hypoxia, with SpO2 90 percent as the accepted floor. HFNC is stepped up only after two hours of low-flow failure, and bronchodilators are not indicated under 12 months. Aggressive early HFNC does not reduce ICU admission and delays escalation to appropriate senior review.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90 percent, not 92 to 94.
Low-flow nasal prong oxygen is first-line; HFNC after 2 hours of failure.
Salbutamol is not recommended under 12 months.
NGT feeds are preferred over IV in mild to moderate dehydration.
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis pathway targets SpO2 90 percent on low-flow nasal cannula 1 to 2 L/min before considering HFNC after 2 hours; do not chase 94 to 98 percent saturations.

options.rationale: HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after 2 hours per RCH; jumping straight to HFNC bypasses the guideline step. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
RCH bronchiolitis target is SpO2 90 percent, not 94 to 98; facemask flow is also excessive first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
RCH CPG makes low-flow nasal cannula the first-line oxygen delivery in bronchiolitis with SpO2 90 percent as the target; HFNC only after 2 hours of low-flow failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months as beta-2 receptor density is insufficient for benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Hypertonic saline is not routinely used in Australian bronchiolitis pathways, and off-oxygen management with SpO2 87 percent is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: The RCH croup pathway separates mild and severe management by dexamethasone dose. Mild and moderate croup receive 0.15 mg/kg orally as a single dose; severe croup receives 0.6 mg/kg orally with nebulised adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline requires a minimum three-hour observation window because of rebound stridor risk after the effect wears off. Prednisolone is not recommended as an alternative because relapse rates are higher.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally, single dose.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally plus nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 is a flat dose (not per kg).
Minimum three-hour observation after last adrenaline dose.
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally is the RCH default for mild to moderate croup; escalate to 0.6 mg/kg only when stridor is present at rest with recessions.

options.rationale: Prednisolone has been shown less effective than single-dose dexamethasone for croup and is not the AU first-line agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
RCH CPG uses dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild and moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
0.6 mg/kg is the severe-croup dose per RCH; a Westley score of 2 is mild and does not require it. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Nebulised budesonide is a fallback if oral dexamethasone is refused or vomited; oral is preferred first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor at rest, not mild presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary:
Viral gastroenteritis damages the small bowel brush border, where lactase sits most superficially, so lactose passes undigested into the colon and is fermented. The result is explosive, acidic, watery stool with perianal excoriation that recurs with every lactose containing feed and stool that is acidic with reducing substances. It is transient, and a few weeks of lactose free formula followed by reintroduction is enough. Persisting symptoms after that, or faltering growth, blood in the stool or systemic features, move the problem into a different diagnostic category.

In context: most post-gastroenteritis diarrhoea resolves without intervention within a fortnight. The features that separate them are growth, the presence of blood or mucus, and whether symptoms track a specific feed. A thriving child whose symptoms follow the bottle has an osmotic, enzymatic problem; a child losing weight or passing blood does not.
key_points: Transient lactase deficiency follows mucosal injury from gastroenteritis
Acidic stool with reducing substances supports the diagnosis
Treat with lactose free formula for a few weeks, then reintroduce
Faltering growth or blood in stool points elsewhere
explanation.pearls: Diarrhoea that reappears with every bottle in a thriving toddler is an enzyme problem; diarrhoea that continues regardless of what goes in is not.

options.rationale: Acidic stool with reducing substances after gastroenteritis indicates transient lactase deficiency from brush border injury; a short course of lactose free formula with review is the RCH approach while the mucosa recovers. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Extensively hydrolysed formula is for cow milk protein allergy, suggested by blood or mucus in the stool, eczema, poor growth or vomiting on exposure rather than by acidic osmotic stools. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Metronidazole treats confirmed giardiasis, which typically causes prolonged foul diarrhoea with bloating and weight loss rather than a strictly formula related pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Soy formula and allergy assessment suit an infant with an immune mediated reaction to cow milk protein, and soy is generally avoided under 6 months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Coeliac serology is indicated for a child with chronic diarrhoea, faltering growth or anaemia after gluten exposure, and this boy is growing normally with a clear temporal trigger. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses a banded IM adrenaline table rather than mg/kg calculation to reduce dose errors under stress. The 7.5 to 20 kg band receives 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr), and 20 kg and above receives 300 micrograms (EpiPen). IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses fail and requires cardiac monitoring. Nebulised adrenaline is a symptomatic adjunct for airway oedema only.
key_points: 7.5 to 20 kg: EpiPen Jr 150 micrograms IM.
20 kg and above: EpiPen 300 micrograms IM.
Banded dosing beats mg/kg arithmetic under stress.
IV adrenaline reserved for refractory cases with monitoring.
explanation.pearls: ASCIA banded adrenaline: 150 mcg for 7.5 to 20 kg, 300 mcg for 20 kg and above; the mg/kg calculation is a distraction that causes dose errors.

options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded IM adrenaline: 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr) for 7.5 to 20 kg body weight; this child is 15 kg. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
300 microgram EpiPen is the ASCIA band for 20 kg and above; overdose in a 15 kg child risks tachyarrhythmia. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis with cardiac monitoring after two IM doses have failed. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptomatically only and does not reverse systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
ASCIA uses banded dosing not mg/kg arithmetic to reduce dose errors; 75 micrograms is under-dosed and is not a recognised band. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Fever in an infant under three months usually triggers a full evaluation with blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures and immediate empirical intravenous antibiotics, because clinical assessment alone cannot exclude invasive bacterial infection at that age. A clearly identified viral focus modifies that rule above one month: infants aged one to three months with clinical bronchiolitis, particularly with a confirmed respiratory virus, have a rate of bacteraemia and meningitis close to zero, so a lumbar puncture and empirical antibiotics are not routinely required. The one infection that is not excluded is urinary tract infection, which runs at several per cent in this group, so a catheter or suprapubic specimen is still collected. Infants under one month, and any infant who looks unwell, has apnoeas or is poorly perfused, get the full evaluation regardless of the virus result. In context, bronchiolitis is the commonest reason for admission of Australian infants in winter, and its management is supportive: oxygen and feeding support, with no role for bronchodilators, corticosteroids or antibiotics.
key_points: Under one month of age, fever means the full evaluation whatever the virus result.
One to three months with clinical bronchiolitis: bacteraemia and meningitis risk is very low.
Concurrent urinary tract infection is not excluded and needs a catheter specimen.
Any infant who is unwell or apnoeic gets the full evaluation regardless.
explanation.pearls: A positive respiratory virus swab lowers the probability of invasive bacterial infection but never of urinary tract infection, which is why the urine specimen survives every version of this pathway.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.rationale: A well-perfused infant older than one month with clinical bronchiolitis and a confirmed viral cause has a very low risk of bacteraemia or meningitis, but the risk of concurrent urinary tract infection persists, so a catheter specimen is sent and he is observed for feeding and respiratory work. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.rationale: The full evaluation is mandatory under one month of age, and above that for any infant who is unwell, poorly perfused or has no identified focus for the fever. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.rationale: Starting antibiotics before cerebrospinal fluid is obtained is justified when the infant is shocked or the lumbar puncture must be deferred, neither of which applies here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics would follow a focal bacterial infection such as lobar pneumonia with focal signs and a consistent chest radiograph. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Discharge without a urine specimen would be reasonable in an older infant beyond three months with bronchiolitis who is feeding normally. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death in paediatric DKA and typically emerges 4 to 12 hours into rehydration. Warning signs include falling GCS, new headache, bradycardia, hypertension, and pupillary changes. The APEG and RCH DKA pathways specify immediate mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 15 minutes (or hypertonic saline 3 percent 2.5 to 5 mL/kg) and a reduction in fluid rate on presumptive cerebral oedema. Isotonic fluids and delayed insulin (one hour after fluid start) are used across the whole rehydration phase to minimise osmolar shift.
key_points: Falling GCS plus headache mid-rehydration is cerebral oedema until proven otherwise.
Mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV over 15 minutes is first-line.
Isotonic fluids only until glucose below 15 mmol/L.
Bicarbonate is not used in paediatric DKA unless pH under 6.9 with shock.
explanation.pearls: Neurological deterioration during paediatric DKA rehydration is cerebral oedema; mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV within minutes and halve the fluid rate.

sources.label: APEG DKA in children and adolescents 2020

options.rationale: Further boluses in a child with a falling GCS and worsening headache during DKA rehydration risk precipitating overt cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; APEG DKA guidelines)

Deteriorating GCS with headache mid-rehydration is presumptive cerebral oedema; RCH and APEG recommend immediate mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 15 minutes and fluid rate reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Insulin without addressing the cerebral event and while GCS is falling does not treat the emergent problem; APEG delays insulin one hour after fluid start regardless. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

Sodium bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is associated with cerebral oedema and is not indicated at pH 7.11; it is reserved for pH under 6.9 with cardiovascular compromise. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)
Hypotonic fluids in early DKA rehydration accelerate cerebral oedema risk; RCH keeps isotonic fluids until glucose falls below 15 mmol/L. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: RCH deliberately narrowed UTI imaging following evidence that most abnormalities were antenatally detected. A single typical UTI in a well child under 24 months, responding to antibiotics with normal antenatal scans, needs no imaging. Illness-phase ultrasound is reserved for atypical features (poor response, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine). DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and not routine in the RCH pathway.
key_points: Typical UTI plus normal antenatal scans equals no imaging.
Illness-phase ultrasound only for atypical UTI features.
DMSA and MCUG are not routine in RCH.
Follow-up ultrasound only for recurrent UTI or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Under RCH, a typical E coli UTI in a well child under 24 months with normal antenatal scans needs no imaging; do not default to DMSA or MCUG.

options.rationale: RCH restricts illness-phase renal ultrasound to atypical UTI: poor response to 48 h antibiotics, non E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
MCUG is a NICE construct, not part of the RCH pathway for a single typical UTI; do not order routinely. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
RCH does not require imaging after a single typical UTI even under 24 months when antenatal scans were normal; safety net for recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
DMSA is not part of the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI; it is a NICE tool, not AU standard practice here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
Routine post-infection ultrasound is not required for a single typical UTI under 24 months per RCH when antenatal monitoring was normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is common in preschool children and easily missed because fewer than 4 principal features are present. AHA and RCH algorithms treat when fever exceeds 5 days plus 2 or 3 principal features and supportive labs (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, platelets over 450 after day 7, albumin under 30, elevated ALT, WCC over 15, sterile pyuria) OR any coronary Z score over +2.5. IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours plus aspirin is standard first-line, and the treatment window is within the first 10 days of fever to minimise aneurysm risk.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on lab criteria plus coronary imaging.
IVIG 2 g/kg is the definitive treatment; aspirin is adjunct.
Coronary Z score over +2.5 alone meets treatment criteria.
Steroids are added, not substituted, in high risk cases.
explanation.pearls: In fever over 5 days with cracked lips, non-purulent conjunctivitis and a raised CRP, do not wait for the fifth criterion; check LAD Z score and give IVIG 2 g/kg if any coronary dilation is present.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement 2017: Diagnosis and Treatment of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Fever over 5 days plus 3 principal features and supportive labs (CRP over 30, platelets over 450, sterile pyuria, ALT elevation, albumin under 30) plus a coronary Z score over +2.5 meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria and mandates IVIG within 10 days of fever onset per the RCH pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
The AHA and RCH algorithms explicitly treat incomplete disease that meets supplementary lab criteria plus coronary changes; delay increases aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first-line in Australia; steroids are used with IVIG in high risk groups (Kobayashi score high, under 12 months, coronary dilation at diagnosis), not alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Blood culture is negative, and the syndrome is not compatible with occult sepsis; antibiotics do not treat the underlying vasculitis and delay definitive care. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Coronary dilation is already present and the risk of progression to aneurysm is highest within the first 10 days; discharge would miss the treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: The Australian bilirubin nomogram plots serum bilirubin against postnatal age in hours and adjusts thresholds for risk factors including DAT-positive isoimmune haemolysis. A DAT-positive infant with ABO incompatibility at 28 hours postnatal is high risk; phototherapy is initiated well below the standard line. IVIG and exchange transfusion escalate only if bilirubin continues to rise on maximal phototherapy or approaches the exchange line. Reassessment at 6 hours confirms response.
key_points: DAT-positive haemolysis lowers the phototherapy threshold.
Age-in-hours nomogram is the standard, not fixed bilirubin cutoffs.
IVIG is second-line if bilirubin keeps rising on intensive phototherapy.
Exchange transfusion is reserved for failure of maximum medical therapy.
explanation.pearls: A DAT-positive ABO baby with bilirubin over 250 micromol/L in the first 24 to 48 hours crosses the intensive phototherapy line on the RCH nomogram; start phototherapy immediately and recheck within 6 hours.

options.rationale: A bilirubin of 260 micromol/L at 28 hours in an ABO incompatible DAT-positive infant is well above the phototherapy line; observation alone risks kernicterus. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

At 28 hours in a haemolytic infant the treatment line sits close to 240 micromol/L; intensive phototherapy is indicated and response reassessed within 6 hours per the RCH nomogram. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Exchange transfusion in a stable term infant requires bilirubin to cross the exchange line despite phototherapy or the bilirubin/albumin ratio to exceed threshold; not yet indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)
IVIG is reserved for isoimmune haemolysis when bilirubin continues to rise despite intensive phototherapy or approaches the exchange line; not first-line here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)
Feed supplementation without phototherapy does not adequately lower bilirubin in haemolytic disease and delays effective treatment; overnight recheck is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: The RCH UTI cascade in infants distinguishes typical from atypical UTI. Typical UTI (E coli, sensitive to first-line antibiotics, response within 48 hours, no sepsis, no abdominal mass, normal creatinine) requires renal ultrasound only if the child is under 6 months without documented antenatal imaging or if infections recur. Documented normal antenatal anatomy in an infant with a typical UTI removes the ultrasound requirement. DMSA and MCUG are not routine in the RCH pathway; they are NICE constructs.
key_points: Typical UTI in an infant does not always require imaging.
Documented normal antenatal ultrasound removes the routine US indication.
DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH cascade for typical UTI.
Atypical features trigger US during the acute illness.
explanation.pearls: The RCH pathway asks two questions after a first UTI: was it atypical, and was there documented antenatal imaging; if the answers are no atypical features and yes to antenatal imaging, no follow-up imaging is required.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infections in children

options.rationale: MCUG is not routine in the RCH pathway after a first typical UTI; it is considered only when renal ultrasound is abnormal or infections recur. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
DMSA is a NICE construct and is not part of the routine RCH cascade after a first typical UTI in an infant with documented antenatal imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

For a first typical UTI in an infant under 6 months who responded within 48 hours and had documented normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH does not recommend routine repeat imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

RCH reserves post-illness ultrasound for infants without documented antenatal imaging or with atypical UTI; documented normal antenatal scan makes this unnecessary. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Contrast voiding urosonography is not part of the standard AU cascade for a first typical UTI and is unnecessary given normal antenatal anatomy and rapid response. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis is the main long-term complication and can present up to 6 months after the acute illness. Australian surveillance uses weekly blood pressure and urinalysis for the first 2 months, then monthly to 6 months from presentation. Renal referral is triggered by persistent proteinuria, hypertension, macroscopic haematuria, or falling GFR. Steroids do not prevent onset of nephritis and are reserved for established significant renal disease or severe extrarenal symptoms.
key_points: HSP nephritis can develop up to 6 months after acute illness.
Weekly BP and urinalysis for 2 months then monthly to 6 months.
Steroids do not prevent nephritis onset.
Renal referral is triggered by proteinuria, hypertension or falling GFR.
explanation.pearls: After HSP, teach the family to bring the child weekly for BP and urine dipstick for 2 months and monthly to 6 months; refer only when protein persists on formal urine protein to creatinine ratio, BP rises above the 95th centile, or haematuria becomes macroscopic.

options.rationale: HSP nephritis can develop up to 6 months after acute presentation; discharge at 3 weeks misses late-onset nephritis and abandons the standard surveillance window. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
Biopsy is reserved for persistent significant proteinuria, hypertension or falling GFR; not indicated with trace protein and no other features. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
Steroids do not prevent HSP nephritis onset; they are used only in established significant renal disease or severe extrarenal symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

RCH recommends weekly BP and urinalysis for the first 2 months then monthly to 6 months; late-onset nephritis is uncommon after 6 months if surveillance is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

ACE inhibitors are used for established persistent proteinuria; prophylactic use in asymptomatic children with only trace protein at 3 weeks is not recommended. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Paediatric migraine prophylaxis is offered when headaches occur more than 4 to 6 times per month or cause significant disability. Propranolol is first-line for most adolescents; it is favoured over topiramate in adolescent girls of childbearing potential because topiramate is teratogenic and causes cognitive slowing. Riboflavin, magnesium and coenzyme Q10 have supporting evidence and are often trialled together. Pattern reminder placeholder blocks retained here for parity.
key_points: Prophylaxis is offered for 4 or more disabling attacks per month.
Propranolol is first-line in adolescents including girls of childbearing potential.
Topiramate is teratogenic; avoid as first choice in girls.
Triptans are acute abortives, not preventives.
explanation.pearls: For an adolescent girl with 6 or more migraine days a month, start propranolol 10 mg twice daily and reassess at 8 weeks; reserve topiramate for propranolol failure or asthma coexistence.

options.rationale: Propranolol is a first-line paediatric migraine prophylactic per Australian consensus and is favoured over topiramate for adolescent girls because it avoids cognitive side effects and pregnancy-related teratogenicity. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
Topiramate is effective but is teratogenic and causes cognitive side effects; propranolol is preferred first-line in adolescent girls of childbearing potential. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
Amitriptyline is second-line paediatric prophylaxis; use follows failure or intolerance of first-line beta blockade or riboflavin trial. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
Triptans are acute abortive agents, not prophylactics; daily use risks medication overuse headache and is not evidence-based prevention. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
MRI is not indicated where examination and history are typical of migraine without red flags; scanning does not change management and delays effective prophylaxis. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening for CF is a three-tier process: IRT, targeted CFTR mutation panel, then sweat chloride. Sweat testing is diagnostic and required even when two variants are identified because R117H-7T is a variable-consequence mutation whose phenotype cannot be predicted from genotype alone. Sweat chloride requires the infant to weigh at least 3 kg to obtain an adequate sweat volume. A value 60 mmol/L or above is diagnostic; 30 to 59 mmol/L is intermediate and warrants CF clinic follow-up; 29 mmol/L or below excludes CF.
key_points: Sweat chloride is diagnostic; NBS is screening only.
Cut-offs: 60 or above diagnostic, 30 to 59 intermediate, 29 or below excludes.
Minimum 3 kg body weight for adequate sweat volume.
Faecal elastase determines pancreatic sufficiency after diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: In a screen-positive baby with a variable-consequence CFTR variant like R117H-7T, sweat chloride is mandatory to phenotype the infant; a diagnosis cannot be made or excluded on genotype alone.

sources.label: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care
Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Consensus: Diagnosis of CF

options.rationale: Repeat IRT is not diagnostic; sweat chloride is the confirmatory test once screen and genotype are abnormal. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.rationale: Sweat chloride by pilocarpine iontophoresis is the diagnostic gold standard; a value 60 mmol/L or above confirms CF, 30 to 59 mmol/L is intermediate and 29 mmol/L or below excludes CF. Requires at least 3 kg body weight. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.rationale: Faecal elastase is used to determine pancreatic sufficiency once CF is diagnosed; it is not a diagnostic test for CF. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.rationale: Nasal PD is reserved for borderline or complex cases after sweat chloride, not first-line diagnostic confirmation. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.rationale: HRCT is not part of diagnostic confirmation; screening imaging in early infancy carries radiation and does not establish the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
